```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
```

When the same model describes many individuals, subjects, cells or cell lines, their parameters
differ but are not unrelated. A mixed-effects model writes each individual parameter as a
population value plus a random deviation, estimates the population values and the spread of the
deviations, and integrates the deviations out of the likelihood. In dMod2 the random effects are
declared in the `parfn`, and `em()` fits the model by one of four approximations of that integral,
all of them instances of the EM algorithm. The example is the theophylline data set: twelve
subjects, one oral dose each, plasma concentrations over a day.

```{r}
library(dMod2)
options(dMod2.outdir = file.path(tempdir(), "guide-mixed-effects"))
dir.create(getOption("dMod2.outdir"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Model

The dose goes into a depot and is absorbed into the central compartment of volume $V$, from which
it is cleared. Elimination is a flux $\mathrm{Cl}\, C_c$ in the unit frame, so that the clearance
$\mathrm{Cl}$ is a volume per time and the concentration falls at the rate $\mathrm{Cl}/V$.

```{r}
reactions <- eqnlist() |>
  assignCompartment(Ag = "depot") |>
  assignCompartment(Cc = "central", volume = "V") |>
  setCompartmentVolume(unit = "1") |>
  addReaction("Ag", "Cc", "Ka * Ag", "absorption") |>
  addReaction("Cc", "", "Cl * Cc", "elimination", rateCompartment = "unit")
as.eqnvec(reactions)
```

`em()` needs second derivatives, so the parts are built with `deriv2 = TRUE` and the derivative
modes of forward over reverse sweeps.

```{r}
dm <- c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")
x <- Xs(odemodel(reactions, modelname = "theo", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm))
g <- Y(c(cp = "Cc"), x, modelname = "theo_g", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
e <- Y(c(cp = "sigma"), g, attachInput = FALSE, modelname = "theo_e", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE,
       derivMode = dm)
```

## Data

Every subject is a condition. The table of conditions holds what differs between them, here
the dose in mg and the body weight.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
data(Theoph, package = "datasets")
Theoph$Subject <- as.character(Theoph$Subject)
data <- as.datalist(data.frame(name = "cp", time = Theoph$Time, value = Theoph$conc, sigma = NA_real_,
                               condition = Theoph$Subject))
subjects <- sort(unique(Theoph$Subject))
table <- data.frame(ID = subjects, dose = tapply(Theoph$Dose * Theoph$Wt, Theoph$Subject, `[`, 1)[subjects],
                    weight = tapply(Theoph$Wt, Theoph$Subject, `[`, 1)[subjects], row.names = subjects)
head(table)
plotData(data) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [h]", y = "concentration [mg/L]", colour = "Subject")
```

## Random effects

`branch()` copies the transformation once per row of the table, and `insert()` makes it differ
between the subjects: the dose fills the depot, the central compartment starts empty, and the
parameters are on a log scale. An effect formula then turns a symbol into a linear predictor with
fixed and random effects, written as in lme4:

```{r}
trafo <- branch(define(NULL, "x <- x", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "Ag", "Cc", "sigma")), table = table) |>
  insert("Ag <- dose", dose = dose) |>
  insert("Cc <- 0") |>
  insert("x <- exp(x)", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "sigma")) |>
  insert(Ka + V + Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID))
p <- P(trafo, method = "explicit", modelname = "theo_p", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
compile(x, g, e, p, output = "theo")
random <- randomEffects(p)
random
```

Since the formula acts after the log transformation, $\log \mathrm{Cl}_i = \mathrm{Cl} +
\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i}$ with $\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \omega_{\mathrm{Cl}}^2)$: log-normal
individual parameters. The formula syntax covers more:

| formula | meaning |
|---|---|
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| ID)` | random intercept per subject |
| `Cl ~ 1 + logWeight + (1 \| ID)` | a covariate, a fixed effect `Cl_logWeight` on a column of the table |
| `Ka + Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| p \| ID)` | the random effects of `Ka` and `Cl` correlated (same ID `p`) |
| `Cl ~ 1 + wt + (1 + dose \| p \| ID)` | a covariate and a random slope, correlated with the intercept |
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| ID) + (1 \| ID:OCC)` | variability between subjects and between occasions of a subject |
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| gr(ID, dist = laplace()))` | Laplace instead of normal random effects |

A group, a level of the grouping such as a subject, may own several conditions, which share its
random effects; a condition outside every group has none. The random effects of one ID, or of one
term without an ID, form a block with a full covariance, so that $\Omega$ is block diagonal; its
parameters `omega_<a>_<b>` are the entries of the Cholesky factor of each block, log standard
deviations on the diagonal. Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process random effects, which are
exactly zero unless the data need them, are the subject of [chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html);
this chapter treats normal ones.

## Marginal likelihood

For group $i$ of $G$, the transformation gives the inner parameters $\phi_i = h(\theta, \eta_i)$, and
the observation model is

$$\begin{aligned}
y_{ij} &= g\bigl(x(t_{ij};\, \phi_i)\bigr) + \varepsilon_{ij}, \\
\varepsilon_{ij} &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl(0, \sigma^2(\phi_i, t_{ij})\bigr), \qquad \eta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Omega),
\end{aligned}$$

with the population parameters $\psi = (\theta, \Omega, \sigma)$. The sensitivities in $\eta_i$ come
from the chain rule through `g * x * p` like any other, and the likelihood factorises over the
groups:

$$\ell(\psi) = \sum_{i=1}^G \log L_i(\psi), \qquad
L_i(\psi) = \int p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)\, p(\eta_i \mid \Omega)\, \mathrm{d}\eta_i .$$

The conditions without a group add their data $-2 \log L$ as it is. In code the integrand is the
objective of the data, `normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)`, plus the prior
$\sum_i \eta_i^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_i + G \log \lvert \Omega \rvert$ that `em()` builds from
`randomEffects(p)`; `normT(..., df = 4)` in place of `normL2()` gives Student-t residuals.

## EM algorithm

For a reference value $\psi^{(t)}$ and the posterior $q_i(\eta_i) = p(\eta_i \mid y_i, \psi^{(t)})$,
Jensen's inequality bounds the marginal from below [@dempster1977maximum],

$$\log L_i(\psi) \ge \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_i}\bigl[\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)\bigr]}_{Q_i(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})}
- \mathbb{E}_{q_i}\bigl[\log q_i(\eta_i)\bigr],$$

with equality at $\psi = \psi^{(t)}$. EM alternates the E-step, which forms
$Q = \sum_i Q_i$, and the M-step $\psi^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\psi Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$; since the
bound is tight at $\psi^{(t)}$, $\ell$ never decreases, and near the optimum it converges linearly at
the fraction of the information the data do not give. Expectation conditional maximisation (ECM)
[@meng1993maximum] splits the M-step into conditional steps: $\Omega$ in closed form from sufficient
statistics, the structural parameters by optimisation. [Chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html) writes
the same objective on the scale of $-2 \log L$ and minimises $-2Q$.

The posterior runs through the ODE solution and has no closed form. The four methods replace it by
something computable:

| method | posterior and expectation | M-step | reported $-2 \log L$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"focei"` | Gaussian at the mode, one point | trust region on the Laplace approximation | Laplace |
| `"quadrature"` | adaptive sparse grid around the mode | trust region on frozen nodes | quadrature |
| `"laplaceEM"` | moments of the Laplace approximation, nodes of degree 3 | ECM | quadrature of level $K + 2$ |
| `"saem"` | Metropolis draws, averaged over the iterations | closed form and averaged Newton steps | quadrature of level $K + 2$ |

## FOCEI

### Laplace approximation

Write the joint $-2 \log$ density of group $i$ as $\Phi_i(\eta) = -2 \log p(y_i \mid \eta, \psi) -
2 \log p(\eta \mid \Omega)$, with the mode $\hat\eta_i$ and the curvature $H_i = \nabla^2_\eta
\Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)$ of data and prior. Expanding $\Phi_i$ to second order and integrating the
Gaussian gives Laplace's approximation $-2 \log L_i \approx \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_i/2
\rvert - K \log(2\pi)$. The prior is written without its $K \log(2\pi)$, which cancels the last
term, so FOCEI minimises

$$F(\psi) = \sum_i \Bigl[ \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert \Bigr]$$

plus the data of the conditions without a group, the full $-2 \log L$ with every constant of the
data. $\log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert$ is the volume term. $H_i$ holds the derivatives of $\sigma$ in
$\eta$, the interaction of first-order conditional estimation with interaction
[@wang2007derivation; @pinheiro1995approximations], without which the method loses accuracy wherever
$\sigma$ depends on $\eta$. The conditional standard errors of the modes are the square roots of the
diagonal of $2 H_i^{-1}$. Laplace's method is no bound on the integral: its $-2 \log L$ lies above or
below the exact one, by an error of order $K / n_i$ for $n_i$ data points of the group.

### Bilevel optimisation

Every evaluation at $\psi$ runs in C++:

- **Modes.** One trust region per group, Gauss-Newton with an SR1 correction, starts from the modes
  of the last iterate moved to first order along the outer step and ends at
  `innerControl$steptol`. An eigenvalue floor of $10^{-10} \operatorname{tr}(H_i)/K$ keeps
  $\log \lvert H_i \rvert$ defined; the trial points of all groups go out as one batched
  prediction.
- **Gradient.** The modes minimise $\Phi_i$, so by the envelope theorem their shift does not enter:
  $\nabla_\psi F = \sum_i \nabla_\psi \Phi_i \big|_{\hat\eta_i} + \sum_i \mathrm{d} \log \lvert H_i
  \rvert / \mathrm{d}\psi$, with a Newton correction for the gradient the inner search leaves.
- **Model Hessian.** The Gauss-Newton Schur complement $\sum_i [\Phi_i^{\psi\psi} -
  \Phi_i^{\psi\eta} (\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}]$, the Hessian of the volume term
  where the model has second-order sensitivities, and an SR1 correction from the gradients of the
  last three accepted points.
- **Stop.** Where the model gains less than `trustControl$mtol` in the region `rmax`, or after five
  rejected trials that leave the value flat within `ftol`.

### Volume term

$H_i$ has the Gauss-Newton form, so its derivative comes in closed form,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d} \log \lvert H_i \rvert}{\mathrm{d} \psi_k}
= \operatorname{tr}\Bigl(H_i^{-1} \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \psi_k}\Big|_\eta\Bigr)
+ \sum_l \operatorname{tr}\Bigl(H_i^{-1} \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \eta_l}\Bigr) \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat\eta_l}{\mathrm{d} \psi_k},
\qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}\hat\eta}{\mathrm{d}\psi} = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi},$$

from second-order sensitivities, no third. With `control$derivMode = "forward-reverse"`, the
default, every trace comes from one forward pass along the random effects and a backward sweep
([chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html)); the gradient of the volume term is exact, its curvature is
learned by the SR1 correction. `"forward-forward"` takes the second-order sensitivities of
`deriv2 = TRUE` and gives the outer model the exact Hessian of the volume term. The Hessian a fit
reports is exact, forward over forward, where the model has `deriv2`; `summary()` says which. Where
$\sigma$ depends on $\eta$, the standard errors of $\Omega$ from the quadrature fit are the better ones.
`secondOrderCorrection = FALSE` drops the derivative of the volume term, which biases the estimates.

### Fit

`init` holds the parameters that are neither random effects nor created by the effect formulas,
which start at 0; the standard deviations of the random effects start at `control$sd`.

```{r}
init <- c(Ka = 0, V = 3, Cl = 0.7, sigma = log(0.5))
fit <- em(obj = normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e), random = random, init = init, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)
```

The hyperparameters `omega_*` are log standard deviations of the random effects, shown on their
natural scale in the table of random effects. The shrinkage measures how much the data inform
the individual parameters: near 0 the modes spread as widely as the random effects, near 1 the
data of a subject hardly move its parameter.

`value` is $-2 \log L$ with every constant of the data; `valueNonmem`, $-2 \log L$ less
$N_{\text{obs}} \log(2\pi)$, compares with the `OBJ` of NONMEM. The fit holds the estimates in
`argument`, `Omega` and in `omega` the standard deviations and correlations with standard errors,
in `random` the modes of every group with their conditional standard errors, and `etaModes`,
`etaSE` and `shrinkage`. Its methods are those of a fit: `coef()`, `vcov()`, `confint()` (Wald, or
`method = "profile"`), `logLik()` and with it `AIC()` and `BIC()`, `anova()` of nested fits,
`predict()` (individual and population predictions), `residuals()`, `simulate()` and the plots
below.

### Settings

| entry of `control` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `sd` | `0.3` | start of the random-effect standard deviations not given in `init` |
| `innerControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 30`, `steptol = 1e-8`, `mtol = 1e-12` | the trust region of the modes |
| `trustControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 200`, `ftol = 1e-7`, `mtol = 1e-5` | the trust region of the population parameters |
| `derivMode` | `"forward-reverse"` | the second derivatives of the volume term, or `"forward-forward"` |
| `secondOrderCorrection` | `TRUE` | the derivative of the volume term |

`fixed` holds parameters at given values. `em(cores = )` spreads the groups and conditions over
threads, `sparse = TRUE` fits large models with many fixed effects on sparse Hessians, the Schur
complement and the volume term of every group local to its parameters; `"auto"` decides as
`trust()` does. The inner tolerances are tight, since errors in the modes pass into the volume
term and the outer gradient; the outer `mtol` is that of a fit, a predicted change of $10^{-5}$ in
$-2 \log L$. As in any fit, the solver error has to stay below these tolerances.

## Adaptive sparse-grid quadrature

Laplace's method treats $\Phi_i$ as quadratic. Its error biases $\Omega$ most where the posterior is
skewed, for short trajectories such as oral doses sampled near the absorption. A cubature rule
$\int e^{-\Phi_i/2}\, \mathrm{d}\eta \approx \sum_b W_b\, e^{-\Phi_i(\eta_b)/2}$ removes that error
level by level and contains Laplace as its one-node case.

dMod2 combines the nested Genz-Keister rules [@genz1996fully], 1, 3, 9, 19 and 35 points exact to
degree 1, 5, 15, 29 and 51, by Smolyak's sparse grid
[@smolyak1963quadrature; @heiss2008likelihood],

$$A(L, K) = \sum_{\lvert \mathbf{i} \rvert \le L} \Delta^{i_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \Delta^{i_K},$$

with $\Delta^l$ the difference of the one-dimensional rules of levels $l$ and $l - 1$. Level $L$
integrates every polynomial of total degree $2(L - K) + 1$ exactly against the Gaussian, with a
number of nodes polynomial in $K$ (for $K = 3$ the levels 3 to 7 have 1, 7, 19, 45 and 117); level $K$
is a single node, Laplace's approximation. The grid of every group sits on the Gaussian
$\mathcal{N}(\hat\eta_i, 2 H_i^{-1})$ of FOCEI and moves with $\psi$ [@clausen2009maximum]. Some
weights are negative, so $\log L_i$ is summed as a signed log-sum-exp; a sum that is not positive
means the grid does not resolve the posterior, and the evaluation names the group. Gradient and
Hessian are exact, through the sensitivities of the chain.

The fit alternates two steps. A rebuild places the grid of every group at the current $\psi$, at the
lowest level from its stage up whose next level changes its $-2 \log L_i$ by at most `tol` over the
number of groups; levels never fall. A step runs the trust region over all parameters on the frozen
nodes; the nodes of mu-referenced fixed effects, $\phi_i = D_i \beta + \eta_i$, are frozen in $\phi$,
need no sensitivities and hold over larger steps. A stage ends when a Newton step on the rebuilt
nodes would gain less than `tolDecrement` or less than the nodes resolve. `method = "quadrature"`
starts from the converged FOCEI fit. At the estimate an importance-sampling check, a $t_5$ proposal
at the mode on shifted lattice points, flags a group whose two values differ by more than three
standard errors plus the error of its level, or whose Pareto shape [@vehtari2024pareto] exceeds 0.7.

| entry of `control$quadrature` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `tol` | `0.1` | allowed change of $-2 \log L$ by the next level, split over the groups; `Inf` keeps the levels of the stages |
| `levels` | `K + 1` | the stages; level `K + s` integrates polynomials of total degree `2 s + 1` exactly |
| `maxLevel` | `K + 8` | highest level |
| `tolDecrement` | `1e-4` | Newton decrement that ends a stage |
| `maxEcmPerStage` | `10` | rebuilds per stage |
| `cm1Control`, `maxCm1Iter` | `rinit = 1`, `ftol = mtol = 1e-8`; `30` | `trust()` settings and iterations of a step |
| `pruneTol` | `Inf` | drop nodes whose weight lies this much in log below the largest |
| `certificate` | `points = 256`, `seed = 1` | the importance-sampling check, `FALSE` to skip it |

A quadrature fit holds `stageTrace`, one row per rebuild with the stage level, the value, the
Newton decrement, the resolution, the highest level and the number of nodes; `etaCov`, the
posterior covariance $\hat M_i - \hat m_i \hat m_i^\top$ of every group; and `certificate`.
`plotTrace(fit)` draws the trace, and `plotRandomEffects(fit)` the histograms of the modes over the
fitted $\mathcal{N}(0, \Omega_{kk})$.

## Laplace EM

`method = "laplaceEM"` runs ECM. Its first step moves the structural parameters by a trust region on
frozen nodes of level $K + 1$; its second sets every block of $\Omega$ to that of
$S = G^{-1} \sum_i M_i$, with the posterior second moments $M_i = \hat\eta_i \hat\eta_i^\top +
2 H_i^{-1}$, since the modes alone would shrink $\Omega$. It stops when the change of the parameters
and the remaining distance extrapolated from its linear rate lie below `epsEcm` (default `1e-5`),
after at most `maxEcm` (default 200) iterations, and reports the quadrature of level $K + 2$. It reads
its settings from `control$quadrature`.

## SAEM

`method = "saem"` replaces the expectation by draws from the posterior, which need no Gaussian
assumption and cost the same whatever $K$. Stochastic-approximation EM [@delyon1999convergence]
averages the sufficient statistics across the iterations by a Robbins-Monro recursion
[@robbins1951stochastic],

$$s_k = s_{k-1} + \gamma_k \bigl( S(y, \eta^{(k)}) - s_{k-1} \bigr), \qquad
\eta^{(k)} \sim q(\cdot \mid \psi^{(k-1)}), \qquad \psi^{(k)} = \hat\psi(s_k),$$

which converges to a stationary point of $\ell$ [@delyon1999convergence; @kuhn2004coupling].
$\Omega$ has the statistic $\sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top$, and the mu-referenced fixed effects follow in
closed form by generalised least squares. The other structural parameters have no statistic of fixed
dimension: their gradients and Hessians at the draws enter a Robbins-Monro average of quadratic
models, whose Newton step has the score of the marginal likelihood as its fixed point.

Every iteration draws $\eta_i$ by a few random-walk Metropolis steps and independence proposals from
$\mathcal{N}(\hat\eta_i, 1.5 \cdot 2 H_i^{-1})$ [@kuhn2004coupling]; `set.seed()` reproduces a fit.
Burn-in takes $\gamma_k = 1$, lets a variance shrink by at most 5 % per iteration
[@lavielle2014mixed] and ends when no parameter drifts over `window` iterations. Averaging takes
$\gamma_k = k^{-0.7}$ with the mean of the iterates [@polyak1992acceleration] and ends when the
expected rise of $-2 \log L$ from the Monte Carlo error is below `mcTol`. SAEM does not raise $\ell$
in every iteration and never forms it: `em()` reports the quadrature of level $K + 2$ at the
estimate, with standard errors from its Hessian. It is the method for many random effects and for
skewed, heavy-tailed or multimodal posteriors [@kuhn2005maximum].

| entry of `control$saem` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `nBurnin`, `nEM` | `200`, `300` | most burn-in and averaging iterations |
| `nMcmc`, `nLaplace` | `3`, `3` | random-walk and independence steps per iteration |
| `laplaceEvery` | `5` | iterations between refreshes of the conditional modes |
| `laplaceScale` | `1.5` | factor of the covariance of the independence proposal |
| `window` | `25` | iterations of the drift test and of the averaging start |
| `mcTol` | `0.05` | expected increase of $-2 \log L$ from the Monte Carlo error that ends the averaging |

## Methods compared

The same model fitted by the four methods, from the same start:

```{r}
obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)
fits <- list(focei = fit,
             quadrature = em(obj, random, init, method = "quadrature", verbose = FALSE),
             saem = em(obj, random, init, method = "saem", verbose = FALSE))
round(sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = f$value)), 3)
```

```{r}
laplaceEM <- em(obj, random, init, method = "laplaceEM", verbose = FALSE)
round(c(laplaceEM$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = laplaceEM$value), 3)
```

The estimates agree within their standard errors. Each value of $-2 \log L$ is its method's
approximation of the same integral; Laplace EM and SAEM report the quadrature. FOCEI may lie below
the quadrature: Laplace's method is no bound, and a lower value is its error, not a better fit. The
stage trace of the quadrature fit has one row per rebuild, and its certificate the
importance-sampling check of every group:

```{r}
fits$quadrature$stageTrace[, c("level", "ecmIter", "OFV", "decrement", "resolution", "maxLevel", "nodes")]
fits$quadrature$certificate
```

`r q <- fits$quadrature$stageTrace; if (nrow(q) == 1 && q$decrement[1] < q$resolution[1]) "Here one rebuild ends the fit: the Newton decrement on the rebuilt nodes lies below what the nodes resolve, so the estimate of FOCEI stands, with the value of the quadrature." else sprintf("Here the fit takes %d rebuilds.", nrow(q))` `r flagged <- sum(fits$quadrature$certificate$flag); if (flagged == 0) "No group is flagged." else sprintf("%d of %d groups are flagged.", flagged, nrow(fits$quadrature$certificate))` `plotTrace()` draws the trace of a fit with
several rebuilds.

## Diagnostics

Conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) linearise the model around the modes; normalised
prediction distribution errors (NPDE) come from simulations of the fitted model, decorrelated
per subject, and do not depend on a linearisation. Both should look like standard normal noise
against the prediction and against time.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plotResiduals(fit, type = c("CWRES", "NPDE"), nsim = 200, seed = 1)
```

The visual predictive check compares percentiles of the data with prediction intervals from the
simulations, per time bin.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotVPC(fit, nsim = 200, bins = 8, seed = 1)
```

Random effects plotted against a covariate show whether it explains part of the variability:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotRandomEffects(fit, covariates = table["weight"])
```

## Covariates

Clearance and volume usually scale with body weight. The weight enters as a fixed effect on a
column of the table, centred on the log scale:

```{r}
table$logWeight <- log(table$weight / 70)
trafo2 <- branch(define(NULL, "x <- x", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "Ag", "Cc", "sigma")), table = table) |>
  insert("Ag <- dose", dose = dose) |>
  insert("Cc <- 0") |>
  insert("x <- exp(x)", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "sigma")) |>
  insert(Ka + V ~ 1 + (1 | ID)) |>
  insert(Cl ~ 1 + logWeight + (1 | ID))
p2 <- P(trafo2, method = "explicit", modelname = "theo_p2", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
compile(p2, output = "theo2")
fit2 <- em(normL2(data, g * x * p2, errmodel = e), randomEffects(p2), init, verbose = FALSE)
comparison <- anova(fit, fit2)
comparison
```

`anova()` compares the nested fits by the likelihood ratio. Here the weight lowers $-2 \log L$ by
`r round(comparison$chisq[2], 2)`, with a p-value of `r round(comparison$p[2], 2)`: among twelve
subjects of similar weight it explains little of the spread of the clearance, and the simpler
model stays.

## Nested and crossed groups

Random effects over several groupings, nested like occasions within subjects or crossed like
patients and centres, are written as further terms of the formula. `em()` integrates them per
connected component of the conditions, by FOCEI; the [pharmacometrics project](pharmacometrics.html)
fits mavoglurant with variability between occasions this way:

```r
insert(trafo, Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:OCC))
```

Which groups differ at all, rather than by how much, is the subject of
[chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html).


## Multistart

Like any fit, a mixed-effects fit can end in a local optimum. `msem()` runs `em()` from `fits`
starts, perturbed around `init` with the standard deviation `sd`, and returns the best fit with all
starts in `$multistart`. `theophyllineMultistart.R` of the example project `pharmacometrics` runs
200 starts for each of FOCEI, quadrature and SAEM, from the same draws:

```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/pharmacometrics")
stored <- file.exists(file.path(project, "results", "multistart.rds"))
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/pharmacometrics/theophyllineMultistart.R")
```

```{r multistart, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !stored}
cat("> Results pending: `results/multistart.rds` of the project is written by `theophyllineMultistart.R`.\n")
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = stored}
saved <- readRDS(file.path(project, "results", "multistart.rds"))
values <- unlist(lapply(saved$multistart, `[[`, "value"))
wide <- diff(range(values, na.rm = TRUE)) > 50
lowest <- vapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$value < min(t$value, na.rm = TRUE) + 1, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
```

The waterfall of FOCEI, all 200 starts sorted by its $-2 \log L$:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5, eval = stored}
plotValues(saved$multistart$FOCEI, pseudoLog = wide)
```

and those of the quadrature and SAEM, which both report the quadrature, so that their values
compare:

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.5, eval = stored}
plotValues(saved$multistart[c("quadrature", "SAEM")], pseudoLog = wide)
```

All three methods find the same two optima, each at its own $-2 \log L$. Most starts end on the
upper plateau, the fit of the sections above; about `r if (stored) round(mean(lowest)) else "?"` of
`r if (stored) nrow(saved$multistart[[1]]) else "?"` per method reach the lower one, the flip-flop
solution:

```{r, eval = stored}
flipflop <- saved$best$FOCEI
signif(rbind(fit = c(exp(fit$argument[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]), minus2logL = fit$value),
             flipflop = c(exp(flipflop[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]),
                          minus2logL = min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE))), 4)
```

With one oral dose and no intravenous data, absorption and elimination can swap. In the flip-flop
solution the absorption is the slow step, the volume shrinks to
`r if (stored) round(exp(flipflop[["V"]]), 1) else "?"` L and the random effect of `Ka` vanishes.
The likelihood prefers it by
`r if (stored) round(fit$value - min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE), 1) else "?"`,
but a volume of a few litres is not that of theophylline, which spreads through the body water,
about 0.5 L/kg; knowledge of the drug, or a prior on `V`, decides for the upper plateau.

### A variance at its boundary

At the flip-flop solution the variance of `Ka` runs to 0, minus infinity on the log scale of the
hyperparameters, which no method reaches. `em()` refits every normal random effect of its own block
whose standard deviation ends below 0.1 without it, its etas at 0, and where this raises
$-2 \log L$ by at most `control$boundary` (default 0.1) returns that fit, the variance set to 0 and
named in `boundary`. On the lower plateau every method does:

```{r, eval = stored}
sapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$boundary == "omega_Ka_Ka"))
sapply(saved$best, function(b) signif(b[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")], 4))
```

`theophyllineMultistart.R` refits the best fit of every method by every other method from its
estimates:

```{r crosscheck, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = stored}
saved$cross
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = stored}
byMethod <- split(saved$cross$value, saved$cross$by)
quadratureValue <- mean(byMethod$quadrature)
# a bound on the distance of SAEM to the quadrature, one significant digit
saemGap <- max(abs(byMethod$SAEM - quadratureValue))
saemGap <- ceiling(saemGap / 10^floor(log10(saemGap))) * 10^floor(log10(saemGap))
```

From every starting point each method ends at the same estimates and reports its own $-2 \log L$
there: FOCEI about
`r if (stored) signif(quadratureValue - mean(byMethod$FOCEI), 2) else "?"` below the quadrature,
which integrates the random effects more accurately than Laplace's method; SAEM, valued by the
quadrature of level $K + 2$ at its estimate, within `r if (stored) saemGap else "?"` of it.

`msem()` draws every start and seed before the fits are spread over `cores`, so `set.seed()`
reproduces a run; `cores = c(fits = , conditions = )` splits the cores between parallel fits and
threads inside each, as in `mstrust()`. Every start runs to convergence, all at once.
`plotValues()` draws `$multistart` as a waterfall.

## Summary

- Random effects are declared by effect formulas in `insert()` on a branched transformation, on
  the scale the transformation gives the symbol.
- Every method of `em()` is an approximation of EM for the same marginal likelihood: FOCEI by
  Laplace's method at the modes with the exact derivative of the volume term, the quadrature by
  adaptive sparse grids around the modes, Laplace EM by ECM on the Laplace approximation, SAEM by
  Metropolis draws averaged by a Robbins-Monro recursion.
- Build the model with `deriv2 = TRUE` and `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`.
- Check fits with CWRES, NPDE and the VPC, and covariates against the random effects.
